en: He climbed the pass with purpose,
Swaying like a noble maiden.
When he came out upon the pass,
Ask nothing of the hero's bearing.
Before him stood a black rock,
Surrounded by mingled barberry and honeysuckle,
A distant forked black rock.
The noble gray wolf turned about;
Your poor hero, born to surpass others,
Composed himself like a lion.
To tell every detail would be difficult:
Of the many possessions left as a legacy
By Manas, who had gone to the next world,
The most renowned among those objects
Was the great spyglass.
It was a broad spyglass with a hoe-wide mouth,
A great spyglass a full fathom long.
When extended, it lengthened by a fathom;
Its interior glowed red as fire.
It had a handle made of gold,
And your noble mother Kanykey
Had said, "Carry it with you on journeys,"
And made a slanting case worn like a body amulet.
Its interior darkened into clarity;
The tiger's great spyglass
Delighted anyone who looked through it.
Have you heard the tale?
When his khan-father, Khan Manas,
Long ago, the khoja of Kokon,
When he was holding him in humiliation,
And the afflicted ruler in Bukhara,
When he had overthrown him,
When no soul remained to answer him back
And he strode about unopposed,
When Khan Manas held dominion
Over the multitude,
Beyond Andijan
And this side of Namangan,
In the shelter of the Kokon khan,
Upon a yellow plain bright as the moon,
He seized it in a raid.
Its lens was cut from ruby stone
And fitted into its frame;
Its handle was overlaid with gold.
When a small part needed repair,
He granted Bolokbay
A thousand mares from the herd.
When its tube was turned four times,
Its lenses separated into place;
When one aimed and looked with care,
An object seven days distant
Appeared only seven rope-lengths away.
The tiger's great spyglass—
He turned its focusing wheel,
Set it to his keen eye,
Turned its adjusting screw,
And held it unwaveringly to his eye.
Holding it at a slant,
He filled its field of view;
Holding it steadily,
He satisfied his heart.
Now he saw the city
Of that same Khan Akun,
And now he saw all the different kinds
Of people living there.
They displayed surpassing finery,
And loaded their burdens upon camels;
It was a populous garden-land traveled by caravans,
And its people were somewhat haughty.
They were a people resembling the Sarts,
And their name, he learned, was Afghan.
Their trouser cuffs hung loose,
And they wore striped trousers;
At precisely sixty saddle-straps
Their knives had sheaths.
Their shirts lay open upon bare chests;
They were hook-nosed and dark-eyed.
There were people of countless forms;
If you looked closely, Afghanistan
Possessed a beauty all its own.
Even in the scorching height of summer
They wore black hats broad as cauldrons.
They had donkeys, mules, and horses,
And champions of many different kinds;
In plain robes and dark-eyed,
They had a population of countless kinds.
The khan of that Afghanistan
Was a man endowed with sacred power,
The vigorous elder Akun.
The city spread outward in cornered districts,
Its distant limits sharpened beneath the haze.
Afghanistan was a considerable city;
When he properly trained the spyglass upon it,
He saw that it held such a population.
There in the land of Afghanistan
Were mullahs wearing white turbans;
Such was the account of them.
There were khojas in striped robes,
A populace and a khan,
And living souls of countless kinds.
Akun lacked nothing he desired;
Guarding his treasury
Stood black wrestlers in ordered ranks.
The wrestlers had a curious appearance:
Trimmed beards and hairpieces;
Strange indeed were these people.
They spoke a halting, broken tongue,
And followed the Muslim faith.
Swaggering like black stallions,
The people of Afghanistan
Had a weakness for watching women.
Raised in arms without seeing a cradle,
They had long heads shaped like mortars.
They had costly food
Of red currants and raisins.
Their name, he learned, was Afghan;
They were a rather feeble people.
Long ago, when my khan-father Manas lived,
He raided them and took plunder,
Taking elephants among the spoils,
And loading the elephants with gold coins;
He took a thousand dark-eyed women.
To raid them had been fitting,
For it was a rather feeble land;
What they said was true:
Its women were beauties indeed.
If we should become enemies,
And charge into battle,
If they came against us head-on,
We could slaughter them all.
If Kanchoro's wrath were roused,
He could bind and capture their khans.
Baitaylak, man of Khan Bakay,
Could take all of them as plunder;
And Kalyk, man of Sarykan,
Could strike them down like a gyrfalcon in battle.
Shayymbet, man of Jamgyrchy,
Could meet them as an equal,
And if we suddenly joined battle,
If we unexpectedly fell upon each other,
And I charged in with a roar,
Their hearts would fail and they would die;
That wretched, feeble people
Would behold the face of Judgment Day.
They were an exceedingly weak people,
And their name, he learned, was Afghan.
They had houses built with four corners,
And bread made round;
Displaying countless different forms,
Almighty God in his power
Had created them wondrously.
Your lord grew weary of the city.
Holding the spyglass at a slant,
He filled its field of view;
Holding it somewhat lower,
He satisfied his heart.
He turned the right-hand wheel
And directed it toward Opol.
Your lord settled himself,
And from that distant forked place,
He coiled like a dragon
And gathered himself like a white tiger.
That poor, proud-standing hero
Was seized by agitation.
Suddenly growing wrathful,
Your tiger entrusted the spyglass
To his own dear eye,
Toward a spur of broad Opol,
Toward the nose of the mountain there,
Toward the meeting of nine roads,
Toward the expanse of Boru-Koy,
Toward the hollow of Ok-Kyya,
Toward the banks of Great Urgench,
He now trained the spyglass.
Beside the flowing water,
The poor daughter of Akun
Your lord now saw in full.
Your gray wolf, with a fierce appetite
For liquor and women,
Now fixed his eyes intently.
Amid thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens,
He now saw
Churok herself.
He began an uproar;
Your lord of the dark day faltered,
And when he saw Aychurok,
He nearly dropped dead:
"Good heavens, I had thought,
'I took a wife from Bukhara,'
And had gone on believing it;
But instead of taking a wife, good heavens,
I have been living as a bachelor."
Thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens
Moved lightly in their games;
In their midst Aychurok
Glittered like a poppy.
She wore a fitted dress and a sable coat,
With its hem showing below.
Your lord's heart grew tender,
And his mind was deeply stirred;
Each time he looked, Aychurok
Appeared like a precious jewel.
Green-patterned ornaments, powder, and rouge
Of that sister-in-law Churok of yours
Showed upon her bosom;
Each time he looked he gasped,
And your lord's heart opened.
Adorned and resolute,
She swayed as though moving toward him.
Upon her head was a skullcap made of gold;
Her splendor surpassed every living soul,
That poor beauty, daughter of Akun.
